rubric:
STRICT JUDGING RUBRIC: DENIAL AUDITOR (Nebius x NVIDIA Global AI Hackathon, Best Apps & Agents)

How to score
- Section A (gates) is pass/fail. If any A item fails, the submission fails Stage One. Stop there and report it.
- Sections B to E are the four Devpost Stage Two criteria. They carry equal weight and each is scored 1 to 10. Ties go to the earlier criterion, in the order B, C, D, E. Score each criterion from its listed items: every FAIL costs about 1 point, every WARN about 0.5 unless you can defend it to a designer in one sentence, and the score tops out at 6 if any item marked [cap] fails.
- Section F (product invariants) is pass/fail. A failed invariant takes 3 points off criterion B and is reported as a blocker.
- Sections G to K are the design criterion (C) in detail, written for an app screen. Count them inside C.
- Judges might not run the app. Score B to E as they come across in the video, the description and the screenshots, and note when a strength only shows up if you use the app live.
- Judge from screenshots at 1440x900, 768 and 390. If a problem shows in a screenshot, it is real, whatever the code says.

======================================================================
A. HARD REQUIREMENTS (Stage One, pass/fail)
======================================================================
A1. The shipped app makes a runtime call to the Nebius Token Factory inference API (api.tokenfactory.nebius.com). Check it in code on the live request path, not only in scripts or eval.
A2. At least one NVIDIA open model is used at runtime: Nemotron 3 Nano, Super or Ultra, or Super-VL.
A3. The track is set to Best Apps & Agents, and the project is a real app someone would use, not a rebrand of something unrelated.
A4. The public repo URL (GitHub) holds all source, assets and setup instructions. The repo must be PUBLIC at submission. Judges only verify and remind; the user flips the visibility.
A5. There is an OSI licence file (MIT, Apache 2.0 or MPL 2.0) that GitHub detects in the About sidebar.
A6. There is a working demo URL with free, unrestricted access until judging ends (Dec 15, 2026). If live runs need a passcode, the passcode is given in the submission, or the precomputed cases work without one.
A7. The demo video is under 3:00, public on YouTube, and uses no third-party trademarks or copyrighted music without permission.
A8. The text description says how Nemotron was used and where Token Factory sped up the workflow, and lists the other Nebius tools.
A9. The feedback on Token Factory and the NVIDIA models is filled in.
A10. All materials are in English.
A11. It is submitted before Oct 30, 2026, 10:00 am PT.
A12. Tavily bonus, not a gate but checked here: a Tavily call happens at runtime in the shipped app (Aetna policy lookup through search), and the description and video show it.

======================================================================
B. TECHNOLOGICAL IMPLEMENTATION (criterion 1)
======================================================================
B1. Each model is matched to its job and the choice is justified with measured evidence: Nano for fast extraction, Super for criteria and matching, Ultra for referee and drafting. The description or README shows the latency and cost numbers. [cap]
B2. Structured outputs are validated by schema (pydantic). Model output is never trusted for offsets: spans are located again in the fetched text by code.
B3. Citation gate: export is blocked unless every quoted policy line exactly matches text fetched in that session. The demo shows a blocked case working. [cap]
B4. Deadlines come from the fixed rules table, never from the LLM. The code path can be traced.
B5. Policy versioning: the citation names the policy version in effect on the date of service (the CMS LCD as of the DOS). The Aetna snapshot hash is recorded.
B6. Eval: there is a gold set, results can be reproduced (eval/results), recall, precision and agreement are reported honestly with their failures, and an ablation is shown (the Nano single-vote result).
B7. Spend caps (budget.py) are enforced on every Token Factory and Tavily call. Nothing bypasses them with OpenAI(...) or TavilyClient().
B8. The deployed app works. The Lightsail URL loads, precomputed cases render, a live run with the passcode completes or fails gracefully, and rate limiting holds.
B9. The offline test suite passes (./.venv/bin/pytest) with no network calls.
B10. Vote and referee design: 2 Super votes plus an Ultra referee on a split. The video or description explains it and shows one disagreement being resolved.
B11. The drift watcher runs with no model ($0 cap) and is reachable at /api/drift. The UI shows it.
B12. Failure handling: empty model content, schema failure, Tavily miss and CMS outage each produce a stated error inside the block that failed. Nothing crashes and nothing returns a blank page.

======================================================================
C. DESIGN (criterion 2): "complete, coherent product, not a proof of concept"
======================================================================
C1. A biller can go from board, to case, to criteria and evidence, to the appeal or documentation request, to export, without dead ends. Every nav item opens a real view. [cap]
C2. Prevention mode, policy watch and the main denial flow share one shell, one palette and one type system.
C3. Every block has its empty, zero, loading and error state built and reachable (see J).
C4. The product is named: mark and name at the top of the shell, with the scope shown (practice or review date).
C5. Its main job is one click from the first screen: open the most winnable or most urgent denial.
C6. Sections G to K pass with 0 FAIL from `lint.mjs --app` and `inspect.mjs --app`. Every WARN is defended in one sentence.
C7. The video shows the product doing its job end to end in under 3 minutes, with the "aha" (a citation verified against fetched text, or an export blocked) shown on screen.

======================================================================
D. POTENTIAL IMPACT (criterion 3)
======================================================================
D1. The audience is specific (billers at small practices, outpatient MRI/CT denials) and the problem is quantified with figures that cite primary sources. Every statistic in the description and video is traceable (docs/facts.md). Any invented figure fails this item. [cap]
D2. What the demo shows actually solves the stated pain: triage by winnability, the missing-evidence request to the physician, and a draft appeal that a human sends.
D3. Limits are stated honestly: synthetic data only, one CPT family, two policy sources, and a human always sends.
D4. A believable next step or adoption path that doesn't overclaim. There is no "never trained on" claim unless Token Factory's terms have been verified.
D5. Prevention mode is shown as a second value: it catches a weak prior-auth request before it's submitted, and the earliest qualifying date is computed in code.

======================================================================
E. QUALITY OF THE IDEA (criterion 4)
======================================================================
E1. The idea isn't obvious: it's not "an AI that writes appeal letters". The new parts are the citation gate tied to fetched text, versioning by date of service, and turning missing evidence into a documentation request.
E2. The submission shows it understands the domain: CARC codes, LCD L34220, Aetna CPB 0236, and why eviCore, Carelon and ACR are linked but never sent to a model.
E3. The way Nemotron is used is creative and fits the job: code numbers the sentences and the model picks ids, votes and a referee, VL reading the letter image.
E4. The policy-drift watch is shown as an insight: an appeal that was valid can go stale when the policy changes.

======================================================================
F. PRODUCT INVARIANTS (pass/fail, from CLAUDE.md)
======================================================================
F1. Only synthetic patient data appears anywhere: repo, demo, screenshots and video. No real PHI.
F2. Export is impossible unless every quoted policy line exactly matches text fetched in the session. Try it: edit a quote and confirm export is blocked.
F3. Deadlines come only from the fixed rules table.
F4. The tool never submits anything. No "Send" or "Submit to payer" control exists. The copy says a human sends it.
F5. Nowhere does it claim inputs are "never trained on".
F6. No eviCore, Carelon or ACR text is stored or sent to a model. These are links by name only (sources.assert_allowed). UHC is absent.
F7. CPT codes appear as bare codes only, with no AMA descriptors, and the AMA attribution line is present.
F8. The one accent, blue pencil #8EC5E8, appears only where something was verified against fetched text. It is never on chrome, never on a primary button and never decorative.
F9. The board counts every deadline from one review date (api.board_as_of), and the UI states that date.
F10. Public demo: precomputed cases need no passcode, while live runs are gated and rate-limited.

======================================================================
G. SHELL, CANVAS, TITLE (app-screen rules)
======================================================================
G1. One shell archetype is used consistently (open plane, tinted frame, ruled T-frame, icon rail or no sidebar). A dark screen uses one ground everywhere, divided by 1px rules (#222224-ish on #171719) or by nothing.
G2. Sidebar: 210-292px wide (around 230), rows with a 32px hit area on a 34px pitch, 16px outline icons at about 1.5px stroke, 14px labels. The active item is shown by brightness on dark, not a coloured pill or a left bar. Group labels are sentence case at 12-13px, never uppercase. Nav items are other screens, never anchors into one long page.
G3. Counts appear on nav items only for queues that need action, with the noun clear from the label ("Due this week 4").
G4. A top bar, if there is one, holds something real (search, scope or object name) and is never mostly empty.
G5. Each screen has exactly one h1, a noun (not a greeting), at 18-32px and 600-700 weight. Nothing over 32px. An optional 14-16px grey second line states the finding or scope, never instructions about the interface.
G6. One primary action per screen, in inverted ink (light fill, dark label on dark). Actions to the right of the title only when they are real. There is a freshness stamp on data that can go stale (policy fetched at, review date).
G7. One gutter value is used horizontally and vertically. The grid sum is written down and closes. Content runs to the canvas's right edge, with no dead strip.
G8. One left edge from the title to the last row.
G9. Cards in a row share a bottom edge (no ragged-row). No blank band over 40px inside a card (panel-void). A lone card spans. Only an action or a total is pinned to a stretched card's foot.
G10. Narrow blocks (5 columns or fewer, or 6 rows or fewer) don't stretch to 1300px. They run to about 760px and pair with the next block.
G11. Date range or scope is set at page level or per card, never both. Control height in the title and filter rows is 28-40px, one height per row.
G12. No floating button unless it is the one primary action and covers nothing at any width.

======================================================================
H. THE SCREEN'S QUESTION, DATA TRUTH, KPIs
======================================================================
H1. Each screen's one question is written down. Board: "Which denials can I win before their deadline?" Case: "Does the chart meet each criterion of the policy in force on the DOS?" The biggest block answers it and is read first.
H2. Each screen's one finding sits under the title or as the lead figure's subline, next to the action it drives (for example "2 criteria lack evidence; request sent to Dr X").
H3. At 1440x900, every block the brief names shows its header and first rows above the fold. Long lists are capped at 4-6 rows with "View all" and a stated total.
H4. Evidence sits beside the answer: each verdict shows the policy span and the chart quote it rests on.
H5. A fact shown twice is one variable: deadline, days left, DOS, policy version and verdict counts agree everywhere. Recompute every count on the board from its rows.
H6. Every relative figure names its baseline ("12 days left from review date 2026-10-25").
H7. KPIs are type, not tiles: no icon in a circle, no sparkline, no tinted tile. Values are 16-40px (lead figure 30-36 and at least 1.3x its siblings, nothing at 48), labels 12-14px grey sentence case above the values, and units as a smaller grey suffix. One container split by 1px dividers, or no KPI row at all.
H8. One figure, one place: no KPI strip that just repeats the panels below it.
H9. Deltas, if any, have their window in words. Colour says good or bad, not up or down. Zero or undefined is grey.
H10. Counts follow the current filter or view and are recomputed on every switch.
H11. No placeholder data (lorem, Acme, John Doe, "User 1") and no vanity totals.
H12. The trade's own words are used: "Medical necessity not documented", "Waiting on Dr. Rao", "Due Nov 4", "Conservative therapy 6 wk". Never "Items", "Records" or "Status".

======================================================================
I. TABLES, LISTS, STATUS, CHARTS, TIMELINE
======================================================================
I1. Table headers are 11-14px grey sentence case, with no fill band, no uppercase tracking, and a sort glyph on the active column only.
I2. No zebra striping. Row rules, if any, are 1px and 3-7% off the surface (#1b1a1f-ish on #131217), with one extent rule per screen.
I3. Numbers are right-aligned in tabular figures with fixed decimals per metric and thousands separators ($1,240.00). `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` actually changes Public Sans digit widths: verify it.
I4. The identity column (patient pseudonym or claim) gets the most width and is never the one truncated. Truncation is one line with an ellipsis, never breaking inside a word.
I5. Dates are ISO (2026-10-25) where rows are compared, and in words for recency.
I6. IDs (claim, CPT, LCD, CARC) are in IBM Plex Mono at body size. Long IDs truncate to about 8 characters with a copy icon. Mono is used nowhere else: not on labels, ticks or captions.
I7. Status pills are 16-24px tall, text at least 11px weight 500, hue on its own dark tint, glyph plus word, nowrap and flex:none, one status mark per row. A saturated fill only for a rare call to action (a fifth of rows or fewer).
I8. Red is a signal, not a texture: at most one red mark per object, on the overdue or failing fact.
I9. Row actions are one ghost button or ink text action in a fixed trailing column, at the same pitch on every row, never muted grey. The selected row in a list that drives a detail pane takes the --active fill.
I10. Charts or the timeline (prevention waiting periods, deadline runway): one hue per chart, the hue on the main data element, no legend for a single series, 3-5 faint gridlines, no y-axis line, round ticks above the maximum, x labels flat and on one step, reference lines 1px dashed with an end label, the event that matters annotated, and labels that never collide. A forecast or future date is dashed. Four hues at most per screen, never more than six.
I11. Every legend swatch is the mark itself, scaled down, listing only kinds on screen.
I12. Progress or meter (criteria met out of total): true ratio, both ends labelled, no stub at zero.

======================================================================
J. STATES, FORMS, BROWSER SURFACES
======================================================================
J1. Real zero is printed ("0 of 7 criteria missing"). Missing or not applicable is a small grey dash, never "--" at value size. A not_applicable exclusion reads as not applicable, not as met.
J2. An empty section keeps its frame and header, plus one spanning sentence ("No denials due this week."). An empty filter result is designed.
J3. Loading: the final layout, with each value replaced by a flat grey bar at its real size and real row pitch. No shimmer gradient and no layout shift when data lands. A live run shows step-by-step progress in the product's words (Reading letter, Fetching policy, Matching criteria).
J4. Error: shown inside the failed block, one sentence on what failed and when the data was last good, plus a Retry text action. Never a full-screen banner. The negative colour appears only on a small icon or a pill. Errors name the problem and how to recover.
J5. A static or snapshot source says so in one quiet notice: the Aetna snapshot date and the CMS version. A notice tint is never a ground.
J6. Every row and control has hover, selected, keyboard focus and disabled states. A disabled control stays legible and says why (for example "Export blocked: 1 quote not found in fetched text").
J7. Fields: label above the field at 14px weight 500, never a placeholder used as the label, one control height per context. Passcode entry has a clear error and a clear recovery.
J8. Destructive actions, if any, come last, as an outlined button in the negative colour, with the consequence in words and a confirmation that names the object.
J9. Browser surfaces are themed from the palette: text selection, caret, scrollbars, focus rings, underline offset, and numerals in tabular data.
J10. Contrast: every tier that carries words is at least 4.5:1 on its surface, placeholders included. Large text is at least 3:1. On dark, two greys at most, clearly apart (around #b4b4b4 and #949494). Running text in full ink.
J11. Copy: controls name their action ("Export appeal", "Request documentation"). No "Get started" or "Learn more", and no genre verbs (unlock, seamless, supercharge, elevate, effortless, cutting-edge, all-in-one). No "not just X, it's Y", no tricolon headlines, only a handful of em dashes, and no performative labels ("Field notes").

======================================================================
K. TYPE, COLOUR, SURFACES, MOTION, PHONE, ANTI-SLOP
======================================================================
K1. One grotesk (Public Sans) does all the text. The second face (Plex Mono) has one job, IDs. Both are really loaded, with no fallback to the system face (check the inspector's fonts-loaded output).
K2. Six type sizes, far apart. The app range is 4-9 sizes. Weights are about 3. Weight 700 does one job per screen. Tracking is 0, with negative tracking only on large type and never below -0.04em.
K3. Headings fit in two lines or fewer at every width. Body measure is 65-75ch in prose blocks (the appeal draft).
K4. Colour on data and status only. Coloured pixels are about 5% or less (study median 3%). Chrome stays neutral graphite. Status is always hue plus glyph plus word, never colour alone. There is one accent family.
K5. Banned palettes are absent: no violet or indigo, no cream with terracotta, no navy or slate dark, no neon-on-dark glow.
K6. Surfaces are flat, separated by a tone step or a 1px border, never both. Shadows only on things that float (menu, popover, dialog), with offset and soft blur. No zero-offset halo. No glass, no backdrop blur, no gradients on grounds, buttons, cards or text.
K7. Radius is bimodal and chosen once: tight 4-8 or soft 16-24, never a blanket 12. Nested radii step down. There are at most 3 panel radii.
K8. Icons come from one outline set at 14-20px, grey, and are drawn as SVG. No emoji. No icons in tinted squares or circles, none repeated down lists or on top of peer cards, and no coloured icon per category.
K9. No eyebrow or kicker above any heading. At most one tracked uppercase label on a screen. No pill badge above a heading. No section numbers (01, 02, 03) unless they are data (a rank, a criterion number that is the policy's own).
K10. No colored border-left or border-right over 1px on cards, list items, callouts or alerts. No hard offset shadows.
K11. No rows of identical cards except for peer objects: 3-6 across, equal widths, no orphan, no icon on top. Nested cards are always wrong. No hero-metric template (big number plus small label plus accent).
K12. Motion is feedback only: press, hover, focus, a menu or sheet opening, a row arriving. Nothing makes an entrance. No bounce, no loops, no hover lift on every card. prefers-reduced-motion is honoured.
K13. The signature move is concrete and present on the first screen. The "blue pencil" verification mark on verified quotes and citations can be named and pointed at, and it carries the meaning "verified against fetched text". A world that shows up only as a colour scheme fails this item. The world lends only type, palette, density and this one move: no costume of a claims form, ledger paper or a terminal prompt.
K14. Name-covered test: with the name hidden, the screen reads as a working product of its category (a claims or denial work queue), as clean as the best in the category and more distinctive, not as "a well-applied kit".
K15. Phone (390): navigation folds into a 48px top bar with a menu sheet, or a bottom bar. A sidebar takes no more than 30% of the width. 16-20px margins, touch targets at least 44px, text at least 12px. The title stays at 20-24px. Tables become two-line rows below 640px with no fields dropped. One region at a time for list and detail. No horizontal page scroll. The first list row is in the top 60% of the screen.
K16. Tablet (641-1100) is its own band: sidebar folded, tables keep 4-5 columns with sublines, and panels stack when one would be under 340px.
K17. Light or dark is justified by the use scene (a biller at an office desk working long sessions), not by category. The judge records whether the dark choice is defended.

======================================================================
CONFLICT RESOLUTIONS: which rule governs an app screen
======================================================================
R1. Rules and borders: on app screens, the app-screen rules (taste-app-screens.md §13) govern, not the SKILL.md page house rules. Allowed: 1px borders on cards, panels, tables and controls; 1px row rules; dashed lines in chart grids and empty slots only. Hairlines as ornament are still banned (crosshairs, crop marks, ruled-paper decoration).
R2. Monospace: the app rule governs. Mono for IDs, keys and code is allowed (Plex Mono for claim, CPT, LCD and CARC IDs, per CLAUDE.md). Mono as a "technical" voice on labels, captions or ticks stays banned (the craft floor and the page ban both agree there).
R3. Small labels: allowed above values (12-14px, sentence case, at least 4.5:1). The eyebrow or kicker above a heading stays banned. The craft floor calls it an absolute ban.
R4. Cards: identical cards are allowed only for peer objects within the §13 limits. The craft floor's "cards as page structure" and "nested cards" refusals still apply.
R5. Pills: allowed inside rows and beside values. Never above a heading.
R6. Index numbers: allowed only as data (rank, node number, the policy's own criterion numbering). Ornamental numbering stays banned.
R7. Icons: the app rule governs (14-20px outline, one set, grey). The craft floor rule applies too: Unicode glyphs and emoji may not stand in for the icon system. The CLAUDE.md "glyph" on status pills must be a drawn SVG mark from the same set. A text character used as an icon fails this item.
R8. Shadows: the app rule governs. A resting card may have at most a small blur under 8% black. Shadows are otherwise for floating things only. The craft-floor depth rule (offset plus soft blur, no halo) applies to whatever shadows exist.
R9. Gradients: only as an area fade under one line chart (the app exception). Banned everywhere else.
R10. Type scale: the app rule governs. h1 is 18-32px, figures 16-40px, 4-9 sizes. The page laws (very large display type, 4.3x headline ratio, a ceiling of five sizes) don't apply. The CLAUDE.md six sizes sits inside the app range.
R11. Motion: the app rule governs (feedback only, no entrances). The page motion floor (8 or more moving elements, a staggered entrance per section) and the craft floor's "one authored moment" are replaced by this. The signature move here is static: the blue pencil mark, not an animation.
R12. Imagery: the page floor (4 or more real pictures, a moving clip, the "live thing") doesn't apply to app screens. The rendered letter.png or a chart fragment counts as product content, not as imagery the screen needs.
R13. Spacing: the page laws (120-220px section gaps, 16-32px margins with full bleed) don't apply. Use the app spacing (4px base, card gap around 16, padding around 20, section gap 24-64, one gutter).
R14. Colour budget: the Operate mode says "a grey screen with one accent is the category default without its polish", while the app study says colour goes on data and status at about 3%. For this product, the CLAUDE.md world governs: neutral graphite chrome, with colour doing real jobs on status (each hue on its own tint) and the blue pencil as the signature move. The judge FAILS the screen only if colour is either decorative chrome or entirely absent from data and status.
R15. Buttons: one filled primary per screen, in inverted ink (the app and CLAUDE.md rule). The page rule "square or fully round, decided once" still holds: controls follow the card radius.
R16. Headlines: the two-line rule from the page house rules still applies to every h1-h6 on app screens.
R17. Public pages that sit beside the app (the deck, or a landing page if one exists) follow the SKILL.md page house rules in full, including no mono, no rules and no motion exceptions. Interface fragments shown on them carry data-ui and follow the app rules inside.

======================================================================
GATE COMMANDS THE JUDGE RUNS
======================================================================
- node ~/.agents/skills/design-taste-frontend/scripts/lint.mjs --app web/
- node ~/.agents/skills/design-taste-frontend/scripts/inspect.mjs --app http://localhost:8600/ (expect 0 FAIL / 0 WARN, with screenshots at 1440, 768 and 390)
- ./.venv/bin/pytest (offline, must pass)
- Manually: edit one quote and confirm export is blocked (F2); confirm there is no send or submit control (F4); grep for AMA descriptors and the attribution line (F7); grep for eviCore, Carelon and ACR body text in stored or sent data (F6); grep for "never trained" (F5).

Sources:
- /home/aman/projects/nebius-nvidia/docs/brief.md
- /home/aman/projects/nebius-nvidia/.impeccable/critique/taste-app-screens.md
- /home/aman/.agents/skills/design-taste-frontend/SKILL.md
- /home/aman/.agents/skills/design-taste-frontend/references/tells.md
- /home/aman/.claude/skills/impeccable/reference/craft-floor.md
- /home/aman/.claude/skills/impeccable/reference/mode-operate.md
- /home/aman/projects/nebius-nvidia/CLAUDE.md

industry.summary:
I researched 12 vendors with WebSearch and WebFetch, not the deep-research-sub-agents skill, because that skill runs a 13-agent academic pipeline and this was a quick product brief. I then checked the patterns against PRODUCT.md and the current web/app.js. The worklist (worklist()/rowHtml()) sorts only by days left and shows recommendation, service date and reason. There's no dollar value, no work status after a letter is drafted, no outcome tracking and no per-case event log. Each case has a citation gate and a timeline.

The industry leaders largely agree on six things.

1. **Rank the queue by recoverable value or likelihood of payment, not just the deadline.** Waystar ranks denials "most likely to be overturned and paid", Experian's Denial Triage segments them "based on their potential value", and Rivet uses "highest opportunity recoveries".
2. **Show the evidence and the reasoning behind every recommendation.** Availity's engine "shows its work" and every recommendation is "traceable, auditable". Cohere's agents cite "the indication data that maps to medical policy". Anterior shows "relevant record findings and the policy criteria applied".
3. **When a case isn't clearly met, hand it to a person with a sourced evidence packet; never auto-deny.** Anterior escalates "with a sourced evidence packet", and Availity "does not auto-deny".
4. **Prompt for missing documentation before anything is submitted.** Cohere does this with "nudges", Availity with DTR (the HL7 Da Vinci Documentation Template & Payer Rules guide).
5. **Track each appeal after it is created.** Waystar offers "appeal tracking + proof of delivery", Epic's follow-up workqueue has activity logs and alerts, and Rivet has worklists by denial type.
6. **Keep an audit trail.** Anterior records events in an "immutable ledger", and Notable's Flow Compass "keeps an audit trail of everything it does".

Denial Auditor already beats most of the public material on criterion-level explainability and verbatim citation checking; nobody else publicly shows a gate that blocks export. The biggest gaps compared with the industry are:
- (a) no dollar value or overturn-likelihood signal on worklist rows;
- (b) no worked/sent/outcome status loop or appeal tracking after the draft;
- (c) no per-case event log;
- (d) no dashboard of reasons or root causes across denials;
- (e) no confidence or "needs a human" routing language on matches;
- (f) no estimate of time or effort saved.

These are candidates only. Anything beyond the approved plan, such as adding claim amounts to the synthetic data, needs the user's go-ahead.

Public material was thin for several vendors:
- **Epic:** I couldn't confirm any generative appeal-letter feature from an Epic primary source. The workqueue patterns come from University of Iowa Epic training pages.
- **AKASA:** Public pages show coding with "evidence behind every code" and Auth/Claim Status bots, but no denial or appeal product.
- **R1:** Public material covers prior auth in Phare OS. R37 is its innovation lab, not a product. The Humata acquisition was expected to close by Q3 2026 and I couldn't confirm that it did.
- **Infinitus:** Payer-call voice agents; its pages returned 403 and secondary sources were used.
- **Notable:** It lists "Generate appeal letters" with no detail on how.
- **Waystar:** AltitudeCreate's inputs and human-review steps aren't described publicly.
- **Change Healthcare / Optum:** I found no primary source documenting an Assurance denial worklist UI. Optum describes outsourced appeal services instead.

None of these vendors' patterns were invented. Every metric in the references is a vendor claim with no published method, and none should go into the Devpost write-up or the slides as fact.

references.pattern: Worklist ranked by predicted recoverability: 'AI + predictive analytics to prioritize the denials most likely to be overturned and paid'. Denials auto-routed to the right work group; 'Customized, exception-based workflows'.
references.howToApplyHere: The worklist sorts only by days_left, then by verdict order (web/app.js worklist()). Add a second sort key shown on each row: verdict strength (appeal > doc_request > ...) plus, if the synthetic scenario has it, the billed amount. Or offer a 'Sort: deadline | likely to win' toggle. Keep the deadline as the primary safety sort, with the reasoning stated in the row ('appeal-ready, 3 rules met with evidence'). Never show a fabricated overturn probability; derive it only from the fixed verdict rule.

references.pattern: Post-draft lifecycle: 'Appeal tracking + proof of delivery', 'batch appeal submission options', 'Advanced analytics + root-cause reporting', and a library of '1K+ prepopulated payer-specific forms'.
references.howToApplyHere: The tool never submits, but it can track. Add a per-case work status the biller sets by hand (Not started > Letter drafted > Exported > Sent by you on [date] > Outcome: overturned / upheld), shown as a column and filter on the worklist. Add a small root-cause strip above the list (counts by CARC/triage class: administrative / plan exclusion / clinical). Keep 'Sent by you' wording so the human-sends invariant stays visible.

references.pattern: Onboarding and ROI framing through a calculator: inputs are monthly claim volume, denial rate, average claim value and appeal packages per month; outputs are revenue recovered and staff hours saved. It contrasts '38hrs' manual, '12hrs' with AI letters and '2hrs' with automated workflows per 100 appeal packages (vendor estimates).
references.howToApplyHere: On the How-it-works page or the Devpost or deck, show measured per-case time and the cost already logged by the budget tracker (cents per case, pipeline step timings). Don't claim hours saved without measurement; label any estimate as an estimate.

references.pattern: Explainable, traceable recommendations: the engine 'shows its work' by mapping patient data to codified policy logic (CQL), and 'every recommendation is traceable, auditable, and grounded in a health plan's medical criteria'. It recommends but never auto-denies; users can override; pended cases go to a person with 'relevant evidence visually organized for easy access'.
references.howToApplyHere: This validates the existing rule-by-rule board (rulesHtml/ruleHtml). Apply two things: (1) an explicit 'Override' or 'Mark as reviewed' control on each rule, recorded in the audit section, so the biller visibly stays in charge; (2) wording that mirrors 'recommendation', for example 'Recommended: appeal', never 'Decision'. Put the policy sentence and chart sentence side by side in the pended (missing_documentation / split-vote) rows first.

references.pattern: Provider-side bundling of 'denial prevention and denial management', 'Denial management tools to identify denial patterns and streamline appeals workflows', and 'Real-time claim tracking'.
references.howToApplyHere: This supports the two-mode navigation (Denials to work / Before you submit). Link the modes: from a doc_request or not_yet denial, offer 'Check the next request for this patient before submitting', which opens the prevention check with the same policy. That frames prevention as the loop that closes denials.

references.pattern: Two-stage model. Pre-submission, it 'flags claims with a high potential of denial, so the right specialist can intervene before claims go to payers'. Post-denial, it 'segment[s] denials based on their potential value' and 'pushes urgent tasks to the front of the queue'.
references.howToApplyHere: Mirror the two stages explicitly in the How-it-works copy and the deck: Before you submit = prevention, Denials to work = triage. In the worklist, add a pinned 'Act today' group at the top (overdue or <7 days, actionable verdicts) above the sorted list, so urgent items are physically first rather than only coloured.

references.pattern: Line-by-line pre-submission edits with 'alert messages [that] appear in your native work queue', each with 'detailed explanations of why a claim was flagged'. The payer edit library is maintained by a content team.
references.howToApplyHere: For administrative (fix_checklist) denials, make each checklist item say why it was flagged (the CARC code and its plain-English meaning from the fixed CARC table) and what to change. That turns the fix list into scrubber-style explained edits instead of bare instructions.

references.pattern: Confidence routing: 'Confidence scoring automatically updates high-confidence coverage directly in the EHR', while 'flagging low-confidence results for staff review'. Many checks run 'in a single automated workflow'.
references.howToApplyHere: The matcher already has a confidence signal (2 Super votes, Ultra referee on a split). Surface it per rule with an honest label: 'Both checks agreed' vs 'Checks split; referee decided, review this one'. Add a 'Needs your review' filter so split-vote rules surface first. No numeric confidence scores.

references.pattern: Agents 'identifying, extracting, and citing the indication data that maps to medical policy'. Each agent carries a visible autonomy label (Assistive / Automated / Hybrid). 'Human judgment always remains with qualified people for complex determinations.' 'Transparent, auditable outputs', 'Human reviewer benchmarked'.
references.howToApplyHere: Label each pipeline step on the case audit section and the How-it-works page by who decides. 'Code decides' covers quote verification, dates, deadline and verdict rule. 'Model suggests, code verifies' covers criteria, facts and matches. 'You decide' covers sending. This is PRODUCT.md principle 2 made visible, in Cohere's style. Show eval numbers (verdict 83% on 24 clinical cases, gold criterion 93%) as the 'benchmarked' trust signal, with sample sizes.

references.pattern: 'Prompt submitters for missing information during intake', 'Intelligent in-workflow push notifications or "nudges" alert providers/auth submitters to missing attachments', 'Smart Prompts to Boost Approvals', 'Real-time requirement checks'. The portal ends with a 'Request submitted!' confirmation.
references.howToApplyHere: In 'Before you submit', put the missing items at the top of the check as a short checklist ('Add: 6 weeks of conservative care documented; you have 23 days'). Each item links to the rule and to the documentation request. The readiness label (ready / add_documentation / not_yet / doesnt_qualify) stays the headline.

references.pattern: A plain status vocabulary for providers: a request 'may be eligible for auto-approval' and then 'you will see the authorization number populate'. Otherwise it 'may pend for either determination of medical necessity or due to missing information', with review by 'registered nurses and doctors'. Review criteria are published by payer in a 'Payer Information Center'.
references.howToApplyHere: Adopt the 'pend reason' idea: when a verdict isn't appeal, always state which of two reasons applies (chart is missing evidence, or the policy isn't met). Add a 'Policies we check' page listing L34220 versions and the Aetna CPB 0236 snapshot date, mirroring the Payer Information Center. Link eviCore, Carelon and ACR by name only.

references.pattern: Completes work only 'when criteria are clearly met'; otherwise it 'escalates to a qualified human with a sourced evidence packet'. Each outcome shows 'relevant record findings and the policy criteria applied'. Policy interpretations stay 'version-controlled'. Every action is in 'an immutable ledger of events' supporting 'appeals, regulatory review, and internal QA'. Trust signals: SOC 2, HIPAA, HITRUST e1, Trust Center.
references.howToApplyHere: (1) Add a per-case 'Activity' log built from the run JSON: letter read, policy fetched (version + effective date), N rules extracted, quotes verified, gate result, exported at. This ledger is shown read-only. (2) Name the documentation request an 'evidence packet' view that bundles policy line + chart line + gap. (3) The policy-version pinning plus the drift watcher already matches 'version-controlled'; surface it as a trust line on each case ('Policy L34220 v40, in effect on DOS; still current as of nightly check'). Make no compliance-badge claims; there are none.

references.product: Resolute PB follow-up workqueue (University of Iowa Epic training)
references.pattern: Billers work denials in a follow-up workqueue with 'alert icons'. Every action is documented as a 'follow-up activity'. Staff can 'create additional documentation request releases directly from their workqueues'. An appeal packet pairs 'a letter explaining the clinical basis' with supporting documentation, and the workflow makes it easier to 'compile this information and track it over time'. Claim Status Insights show where a claim is in adjudication.
references.howToApplyHere: The doc_request > physician step mirrors Epic's 'documentation request release'. Add a row-level action on the worklist ('Copy documentation request') so it can be done without opening the case. Present the export as an 'appeal packet': letter + cited policy excerpt + chart excerpts list, not just the letter Markdown. Small alert glyphs in the row (policy changed since run, quote failed, deadline <7 days) follow Epic's alert-icon pattern.

references.pattern: 'Detects denials faster than your PM or EMR system', prioritises 'highest opportunity recoveries', gives 'on-demand insights around how to solve specific denials', and 'quantifies the impact you and your team are having'. Tiers: Understand (trends: monthly revenue, denial rates, problem areas) and Resolve (detect and appeal).
references.howToApplyHere: Rivet is the closest small and mid-practice analogue. Add an 'impact' footer on the worklist that is computed, not invented: e.g. '7 appeal letters ready, all quotes verified; 4 documentation requests waiting; 2 not worth appealing (saved a letter)'. The 'how to solve this denial' insight maps to the Next-step pane. Keep that pane prescriptive and first.

references.pattern: A shared database of payer instructions and policies, worklists that assign tasks automatically by denial type, and auto-populated appeal forms and letters (from the GuideFlow and Rivet summaries; the primary PDF couldn't be parsed).
references.howToApplyHere: Filter tabs by recommendation already exist. Add grouping by denial type (CARC class), which is how billers batch work. Treat the cached criteria per policy version as the 'payer policy database' and expose it read-only. Secondary source, so verify before citing publicly.

references.pattern: The agent 'Submits and statuses prior authorizations, cleans up work queues, and appeals denials'. Flow Compass: 'keeps an audit trail of everything it does', 'Your team makes the final call', 'See what broke, why, and how to fix it, with failing runs grouped by likely cause', and a dashboard of hours saved, cost saved and revenue generated.
references.howToApplyHere: For the live-run page and the policy-watch (drift) report, group failures by cause ('quote not found in fetched source', 'policy changed since run', 'budget cap reached') with a fix hint each, instead of raw errors. Show the run cost and duration per step, already tracked, as the run-health dashboard.

references.pattern: Coding output includes 'the evidence behind every code'; 'keep your team in control'; 'You set the threshold'. Auth Status 'checks on the status of auth requests and documents the results', with an 'AI + expert-in-the-loop approach'. No public denial or appeal product.
references.howToApplyHere: 'Evidence behind every X' is the right one-line promise. Use it as the product's single headline idea: 'evidence behind every rule, verified word for word'. The 'you set the threshold' idea suggests a small setting for the soon-due window (currently hard-coded at 21 days in dueState) without letting users touch the fixed legal deadlines.

references.product: Phare OS prior authorization (R37 innovation lab)
references.pattern: It manages 'the full lifecycle of a request through determination, submission and completion': it can 'intelligently identify when an authorization is needed', 'submit complete requests with documentation' and 'proactively track payer decisions', with 'a human in the loop when needed'.
references.howToApplyHere: Show the lifecycle as a visible stepper on each case: Denial read > Policy pinned > Rules checked > Evidence verified > Letter or request drafted > Sent by you > Outcome. The last two are user-set; the pipeline already has these stages. R1 aims at 'zero-touch'. Contrast with it deliberately: Denial Auditor is human-sends by design, and that should be said plainly as a feature for small practices.

references.product: Eva voice agents (benefit verification, PA status calls)
references.pattern: AI agents call payers and PBMs to confirm coverage, cost-share and PA requirements, and to 'check the status of a claim, follow up on a prior authorization request'. A FastTrack copilot lets staff skip IVR and hold. Claims '1 million+' payer calls (vendor figure; primary pages returned 403, so this is a secondary-source summary).
references.howToApplyHere: Out of scope (no calls, no submission). The useful pattern is the structured call script: the documentation request and the 'Next step' pane could include a short 'If you call the payer, ask:' block generated from the template (reason code, policy ID and version, DOS, the specific unmet rule). This is deterministic text, not model output.

references.pattern: Public pages describe outsourced denial-appeal services ('over 1 million complex denial appeals'). A third-party review credits Change Healthcare Denials with 'root-cause analytics tied to prioritized follow-up work queues'. I found no primary documentation of the Assurance worklist UI.
references.howToApplyHere: Root cause tied to the queue: each worklist filter tab could show the top reason codes inside it, so a biller sees, for example, that most clinical denials are CO-50 medical necessity. Don't cite Optum UI specifics; none were verified.

lastFindings.title: The prior-auth check marks both deciding rules red 'Blocks' while the headline says the request qualifies once charted
lastFindings.evidence: The headline tile is amber '◐ Qualifies if charted 07/31/2026' and the coverage path says 'Met once 6 weeks are charted'. Directly below, both rule cards (S16 and S18) wear red '× Blocks' pills, and the policy gutter labels S16 and S18 'Blocks' in red. This happens because `prepMatches(run, c, ch.readiness === "ready")` at web/app.js:1048 passes routeMet=false for every non-ready readiness, so `not_met` falls through to `STATUS.not_met` {tone: neg, label: 'Blocks'} at app.js:36. S16 is the duration-gated rule that run.earliest resolves. S18 ('Progressively severe symptoms') is an alternative OR-route, not a blocker. A judge reads three signals that disagree.
lastFindings.fix:
In web/app.js:
- Compute `const routeOk = ch.readiness === "ready" || (ch.earliest && ch.earliest <= r.planned_dos);` in checkView and pass it to prepMatches (line 1048). Unmet alternative indication rules then show 'Route not used' (quiet).
- Add a STATUS entry `pending: { tone: "warn", glyph: "half", label: "Met once charted" }`.
- In prepMatches, set `show = "pending"` for the not_met indication whose duration threshold run.earliest resolves. If that criterion can't be identified exactly, use the criterion referenced by the coverage path's 'Met once 6 weeks are charted' cell, the same logic coverageHtml already uses.
- Make the policy-gutter labels read from `m.show`, so S16 says 'Met once charted' in warn and S18 says 'Route not used'.
- Keep 'Blocks' (red) for not_yet with earliest > planned_dos and for doesnt_qualify.
- Add RANK for 'pending' next to missing_documentation.

lastFindings.title: The inspect gate still FAILs (R2-6 carried over), and the design docs don't describe the shipped UI
lastFindings.evidence: inspect.mjs: 'FAIL [font-not-dealt] The sheet dealt Hanken Grotesk and Hanken Grotesk, but the page renders Switzer' → 'RESULT: 1 FAIL, 0 WARN — not done.' The dealt font comes from /home/aman/projects/nebius-nvidia/.taste-skill/direction.json (direction 'colour-chapters', fonts Hanken). impeccable detect warns 'switzer; not declared in DESIGN.md typography'. It also gives advisories for the 999px, 16px and 22px radii and rgb(102,102,102) ink. CLAUDE.md requires 0 FAIL / 0 WARN before UI ships, and its design paragraph still describes the dark 'Blue pencil' world.
lastFindings.fix:
This is outside web/, so the orchestrator owns it.
1. In .taste-skill/direction.json, set the dealt `style.tokens.font.family` (and any heading/body font fields) to Switzer. Re-running the deal is not allowed: don't redraw the direction.
2. In DESIGN.md and .impeccable/design.json:
   - Typography: declare Switzer 400/500/600, self-hosted at web/fonts/switzer-*.woff2.
   - Palette: copy the :root tokens from web/app.css, including #666666 muted ink, #EDEDEC ground and #FFFFFF canvas.
   - Radius scale: pill 999, canvas 22, card 16, control.
3. Re-run inspect and detect until both report 0 FAIL / 0 warnings.
4. Ask the user for a one-line update to the CLAUDE.md design paragraph.

lastFindings.title: On desktop, the verdict tile spends a third of its width on a floating 'Next step' label and a lone button, or on a redundant sentence
lastFindings.evidence: In d-case, `.vline` has three cells. 'Next step' is top-aligned at y≈161, while the 'Review appeal' button is bottom-aligned at y≈280, leaving about 100px of empty tinted space between them. On d-appeal the same cell holds only 'Open below. A person reviews and sends it.' (`.box-note[data-here]`, web/app.js:263 and 1069). That repeats the gate's own 'A person reviews and sends this letter'. The tile reads as three equal columns of uneven value.
lastFindings.fix:
Make .vline two columns on desktop (Recommendation | Appeal window):
- Move the primary action (`${primary}`) into the Recommendation cell, directly under `.answer` with 16px gap, and drop the 'Next step' cell and its `.fl` label from the markup at app.js:263 and 1069.
- When the target tab is already open (the `data-here` state at app.js:448), hide the button instead of showing a sentence.
- For checks, use the same structure: Readiness + button | Qualifies on.
- In app.css, set `.vline { grid-template-columns: minmax(0,1fr) minmax(0,1.2fr) }`.
- Keep the phone layout from R2-5 unchanged.

lastFindings.title: The honest confidence signal (Super votes split, Ultra decided) is buried in collapsed rule cards
lastFindings.screen: d-case.png (Drew Exemplar: '13 rules agreed, 1 escalated to Ultra' appears only in the Model calls summary), d-check.png ('8 escalated to Ultra')
lastFindings.evidence: ruleHtml (web/app.js:413-430) prints `CONF[conf]` ('Super votes split; Nemotron Ultra decided') only inside `.rule-more`, which is hidden until the card is expanded. No card shows which rule was contested. Industry references (Experian PAC confidence routing, Anterior/Availity 'pend to a human with evidence') treat 'needs your review' as a core trust feature. The data already exists as `m.confidence === "escalated"`, so this is honest and free.
lastFindings.fix:
In ruleHtml, when `conf === "escalated"`, add a visible line under the status pill (outside .rule-more): `

${g("half")} Checks split · Ultra decided · review this rule

`, in the --muted ink with the glyph. Don't use a new colour, and don't show a numeric score. - In rulesHtml's header span, append ` · ${n} to review` when n > 0. - In app.css, add `.conf-flag { font-size: 12px; line-height: 16px; color: var(--muted); display:flex; gap:6px; align-items:center; }`. - Optionally sort escalated rules first within the same RANK.

lastFindings.title: The appeal letter still reads as a proof sheet: 22 inline source chips and 13 captions break up the text a biller sends
lastFindings.evidence: In 'Response to the denial reason', every quote is underlined (`.iq`, app.css ~439) and followed by an inline chip such as '✓ L34220 · S47' or '✓ Note n2 · 06/15/2026' (`.iq-ref`). That is 11 chips in two paragraphs, and many fall at line starts ('✓ Note n2 · 06/15/2026),'). Each of the 13 block quotes above also carries a caption line ('✓ Verified · matches L34220 · S47'). The gate panel on the right already lists every source. The letter column is narrow (about 470px of text in a 1440 layout), which makes the chips wrap more.
lastFindings.fix: Replace the inline `.iq-ref` chips with footnote markers. - Render `${i}` and give each gate `li` a matching `id="g-${i}"` with the same number at its start. The click, hover and highlight linking stays as it is now. - Collapse the block-quote figcaption to a right-aligned 12px `✓ S47` (glyph plus id, with the word 'Verified' in the sr-only text). - Keep `figure.lq.bad` (VOID) loud. - Widen the letter column: `.appeal { grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) 320px }` with the letter sheet `max-width: 72ch`. - The gate list stays the full proof, so the invariant is unaffected.

lastFindings.title: The worklist lead counts from an unexplained 'review date', so a first-time judge can't parse it
lastFindings.evidence: The lead says '3 ready to appeal. The soonest, Drew Exemplar, is due 10/11/2026, 40 days after the 09/01/2026 review date.' (web/app.js:192-193). 'Review date' is a demo-internal clock (api.board_as_of) that never gets explained. Also, the first row is Peyton Fictive (39 days), not Drew, which looks like a sort bug until you notice 'ready to appeal'.
lastFindings.fix: In app.js:190-195, change the sentence to '3 ready to appeal. Start with Drew Exemplar: due 10/11/2026, 40 days left.' (overdue: 'was due …, N days ago'). Append the clock to the existing meta on the right: '7 denials · sorted by days left · days counted from 09/01/2026 (demo clock)'. On phones the meta line already sits under the filters.

lastFindings.title: The coverage path on the check view mixes pill and plain styles, and has a stray dash and a premature 'Reached'
lastFindings.evidence: In the same strip, 'Route to coverage' and 'Waiting periods' render as amber filled pills ('◐ Met once 6 weeks are charted', '◐ Reached 07/31/2026'), while 'Restrictions' and 'Documentation' render as a glyph plus a bold word. Cell heights and baselines don't line up. 'Documentation: ✓ Complete —' shows a dangling em dash, from `refs || (quiet ? "" : "—")` at web/app.js:386. 'Reached 07/31/2026' is past tense for a date that is only reached if care is charted.
lastFindings.fix:
In coverageHtml (app.js ~350-390):
- Render warn states with the same structure as ok/bad: the glyph, then a bold word in the tone ink. Don't use a pill.
- Replace the '—' fallback at line 386 with an empty string. The dash says nothing when no rule is cited.
- Change the waiting-period label to 'Met 07/31/2026 if charted'.
- In app.css, align the four cells to the top (`align-items: start`), so the labels share one baseline.

lastFindings.title: The type scale has grown to 11 declared sizes (9 rendered), against the house rule of six
lastFindings.screen: all screens; inspect.mjs 'sizes in use 12 / 13 / 14 / 15 / 16 / 18 / 28 / 32 / 36 px'
lastFindings.evidence: `grep font-size web/app.css` gives 12px ×29, 13px ×38, 14px ×7, 15px ×10, 16px ×7, 17px ×1, 18px ×2, 24px ×2, 28px ×2, 32px ×2, 36px ×1. The 12/13 and 14/15 pairs are visually indistinguishable: for example, the rule-card meta is 13px beside 12px chip text, and the gate li is 13px beside 15px h3. tells.md:93 warns about 'nearly equal font sizes'. CLAUDE.md describes six sizes.
lastFindings.fix:
Collapse to 12 / 14 / 16 / 18 / 28 / 36 (plus 24 only for the phone verdict answer):
- 13px → 12px for meta, captions, gate li and .say.
- 15px → 14px for UI labels, tabs and the gate h3.
- 17px → 18px.
- 32px → 36px for page titles; the case name stays 28.
Adjust line-heights to 16/20/26/26/34/40. Re-run inspect and confirm that 'sizes in use' lists six or seven sizes.

lastFindings.title: The Fix & resubmit case looks unfinished: a two-item list beside a large letter image, and a Next step tab that repeats it
lastFindings.evidence: The left column 'What to fix' holds one sentence and two numbered items, leaving about 700px of empty space beside an 880px-tall scan. The 'Open the fix checklist' primary button opens the Next step tab, which repeats the same list. The checklist isn't actionable: nothing can be ticked or copied. The industry reference (Experian Claim Scrubber) shows each edit with why it was flagged and what to change. The CARC line here already gives the 'why'.
lastFindings.fix:
In the fix_checklist branch of nextPane:
- Render the steps as a real checklist (`<input type=checkbox>` per item with a label). Persist the ticks per viewer in localStorage keyed by case id, with every read and write wrapped in try/catch.
- Add a 'Copy checklist' secondary button.
- Add one line: 'Flagged because CARC 29: claim received after the filing deadline (fixed reason-code table).'
- In the left column, replace the duplicate list with a short 'Why no clinical appeal' explanation plus the CARC meaning, and link to the checklist tab.
- Cap the letter image at `max-height: 640px` with the scan scrollable inside its frame.

lastFindings.title: Worklist rows: an orphan '·' at line ends and a chevron cut loose from a wrapped next-step label
lastFindings.screen: d-worklist.png (Drew Exemplar, Kendall Pretend, Val Simulant rows)
lastFindings.evidence: 'Sunrise Senior Advantage ·' wraps with the separator stranded at the end of the line and 'CPT 72148 · DOS …' on the next. On Val Simulant, 'Locate proof of timely filing' wraps to two lines and its '>' chevron sits about 170px to the right at x≈1120, detached from the text, while every other row's chevron follows its label.
lastFindings.fix: In rowHtml, wrap each meta segment in `<span class="seg">` and draw the separator with `.seg + .seg::before { content: "· "; }`, using `white-space: nowrap` on .seg so a separator never ends a line. In app-flow.css, make `.nx-link` `display: inline` with the chevron inline after the last word (`.nx-link svg { display:inline; vertical-align: -2px; margin-left: 4px }`), not on a flex row with space-between.

lastFindings.title: The desktop citation gate clips every quote with an ellipsis and cuts the list mid-item with no scroll cue
lastFindings.evidence: Gate `li` text is truncated ('…history …', 'findings on…', 'documented in th…'). The sticky `.appeal .gate` (app-flow.css:51, max-height calc(100vh - 32px), overflow auto) ends with half a row visible ('He completed a course of physical therap…' sliced horizontally) and no fade or count to show that 14 more items are below. The biller can't read the full quote in the proof panel.
lastFindings.fix: Let the gate li text wrap to 3 lines (`-webkit-line-clamp: 3`) with the full quote in a `title` attribute and on :focus-within. Add a bottom fade mask on the scroll container (`mask-image: linear-gradient(#000 calc(100% - 32px), transparent)`), and a 12px muted footer '22 lines · scroll to see all' when scrollHeight > clientHeight.

lastFindings.title: How it works repeats 'Who decides:' 13 times, and the right column leaves half the page empty
lastFindings.evidence: The 'Models and sources' aside (app.js ~1140-1160) lists each step with a grey second line 'Who decides: model suggests, code checks' / 'code' / 'you', repeated on all 13 rows. The aside ends at y≈960 of a 1935px page, so the right half is blank below it. This is the Cohere-style 'who decides' idea, but it reads as repetition rather than a scannable legend.
lastFindings.fix: Turn the second line into a short tag in its own column, with the same three words each time: 'Code', 'Model, then code', 'You', in --muted ink with a glyph (✓ for code, ◐ for model then code, person glyph for you). Put a single legend line above the list: 'Who decides each step'. Make the aside `position: sticky; top: 24px` so it stays beside the steps while the page scrolls.
